questions.prompt: What can you do with a value of type `string | number` before narrowing it?

options.text: Only operations valid for both string and number

questions.explanation: Until you narrow, only operations valid for every member of the union are allowed; member-specific methods require narrowing first.

questions.prompt: Why does `let x = 'active'` have type `string` while `const x = 'active'` has type `'active'`?

options.text: let can be reassigned, so the literal widens to string; const can't change, so the literal type is kept
const always widens; let keeps literals

questions.explanation: A reassignable let widens the literal to its general type; a const keeps the narrow literal type because it can never change.

questions.prompt: A type made of exact allowed values like 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg' is called a union of ______ types. (one word)
questions.explanation: A union of literal types restricts a value to a fixed set of exact options, like a drop-down menu.

questions.prompt: Which operator is the first tool for narrowing a union of primitives?
questions.explanation: typeof narrows primitive unions (e.g. typeof id === 'string' narrows id to string inside that branch).

questions.prompt: Why prefer a literal union over a plain `string` for a size setting?

options.text: It restricts the value to the exact allowed options, making invalid values compile errors
It uses less memory at runtime
Plain string is not allowed as a parameter type

questions.explanation: A literal union turns a free-text string into a fixed set of choices, so an invalid value is caught at compile time.

questions.prompt: How can you force the compiler to require handling of every member of a literal union?

options.text: Use it as the key type of a Record, e.g. Record<Status, string>
There is no way to enforce this

questions.explanation: Record<Status, string> requires an entry for every member of Status, so omitting one is a compile error.
